notes: The opening names trace successive generations. At Noah the list branches into Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Later “sons” can refer to peoples or more distant descendants.
Chronicles has Diphath, Rodanim, Meshech, and Ebal in places where Genesis’ family table has some different forms. The local names are preserved.
Peleg’s name is connected with division. The verse does not specify a geological event or explain exactly how the earth was divided.
Timna appears in this compressed list; Genesis 36:12 identifies her as Eliphaz’s concubine and Amalek’s mother. Chronicles’ wording is not expanded to reproduce that account.
The Hebrew here has Dishon, though the corresponding branch is called Dishan in verse 38 and Genesis 36:28.
vocabulary: Egypt
The Hebrew name Mizraim is also the usual name for Egypt.
Concubine
A woman in a recognized household sexual relationship with status distinct from a principal wife.
Chief
A leader of an Edomite clan or territorial group.

notes: Achar resembles the Hebrew word for bringing trouble. Joshua calls him Achan. His offense concerns property devoted to destruction.
David is listed as Jesse’s seventh son here; Samuel’s account presents eight sons. The list is not expanded with an invented name.
The Hebrew syntax around Azubah and Jerioth is difficult, and the referent of “her sons” is not explicit. Both names and the uncertainty are retained.
The pinned wording can be read as the place Caleb-ephrathah. Other construals rearrange the relationship between Caleb and Ephrathah; the draft does not silently adopt them.
Ahlai is introduced with the flexible term “sons/descendants.” Verse 34 explicitly says Sheshan had daughters but no sons.

The Hebrew has singular “son of Hur,” which can attach to Caleb as rendered. Reading a new heading, “the sons of Hur,” would connect the names differently. The tension with Hur’s earlier descent from Caleb is not silently repaired.
vocabulary: Father of a town
In these records, father can identify an ancestor, founder, or leading clan associated with a settlement, rather than the biological father of a place.
Scribes
People trained in writing and the preservation or administration of records.

notes: Daniel is the name here for David’s second son; 2 Samuel 3:3 has Chileab. Bath-shua and Ammiel in verse 5 also differ in form from names in Samuel.
Elishama and Eliphelet each occur twice in verses 6–8. The nine-name total is retained; no repeated name is deleted.
The second “his son” is compressed and its attachment is disputed. Kings identifies its last reigning Zedekiah as Jehoiachin’s uncle; this verse is not silently changed to match.
The word rendered “the captive” can instead be read as the personal name Assir.
Zerubbabel is listed as Pedaiah’s son here. Other passages call him Shealtiel’s son. The text does not explain the relationship.
The Hebrew gives six after listing five sons of Shemaiah. Shemaiah himself may be included in the total, but the wording is left as transmitted.
vocabulary: His son
In verses 10–14, repeated “his son” advances through successive generations.
Jeconiah
Another form of the name of Jehoiachin, the king taken to Babylon.

notes: The Hebrew says “father of Etam” in a difficult construction. Some readings supply “sons”; the draft signals the relationship without pretending the wording is clear.

Jabez’s name and his mother’s pain are linked to his request to be free from pain. The final phrase can also be understood as asking not to cause pain. This personal request and response is not stated as a promise of wealth to every reader.

The woman who conceives is not named at this point. Verse 18 names a Judean wife and Bithiah, Pharaoh’s daughter. The clauses are compressed, and assigning each child to a mother requires interpretation; the draft preserves their order.
“Ruled in Moab” can also be understood as a marriage connection with Moab. Jashubi-lehem may instead be a phrase about returning to Bethlehem. The Hebrew is uncertain.
The pinned place name is Gedor. It has not been changed to Gerar.
The search for pasture leads to violent displacement of earlier inhabitants. The account’s language of destruction and settlement is retained.
vocabulary: Descendants
The Hebrew “sons” can span several generations in these family records.
Linen workers
A family’s craft is preserved alongside its genealogy.
Simeon
One of Israel’s sons and the ancestor-name of the tribal group listed here.
